second_order: building a small, workable NPR logo together
theme_note: These passages all do the practical work of making one shared logo: choosing a site and size, settling the letter form, refreshing the canvas, placing pixels, sharing templates, and moving detailed coordination to Discord or a spreadsheet. What varies is the mechanism and the design choice—individual pixels, public instructions, off-platform planning, moving, growing, or staying humble and maintainable.

second_order: rallying people to defend the little NPR space
theme_note: These codes recruit and organise protection of the same small canvas space against erasure: calls to arms, coordinates, requests for friends and builders, warnings, and someone taking on an organiser role. They vary from urgent public recruitment to quiet persistence and from manual defense to warnings about incoming attacks.

second_order: working out borders and mutual help with canvas neighbors
theme_note: Across different exchanges, participants claim space, contest who crossed a border, apologise, return rows, grant room, thank neighbors, and help with one another's upkeep. The practice is negotiating coexistence on a shared canvas; what varies is whether it begins with a territorial complaint, stray pixels, a defense request, or an already friendly alliance.

second_order: turning the wall threat into banter, bargaining, and resistance
theme_note: These passages belong to one wall episode in which a hostile-looking demand is answered with tea and mockery, softened into a request to move, resisted on the canvas, and later interpreted by a moderator as space negotiation. The variation is consequential: participants alternately treat the wall as threat, joke, bargain, or defeated attack.
regrouped_from: working out borders and mutual help with canvas neighbors — separated because the wall exchange centered on taunting and resistance before it became bargaining, unlike the reciprocal border work with neighboring art

second_order: celebrating that the NPR logo made it to the end
theme_note: These passages mark provisional and final success, pride, and relief that the logo was intact when the canvas froze. They vary between an early, brief completion, retrospective pride in collective defense, and the participant explanation that lucky timing also mattered.

second_order: finding, joining, and welcoming r/NPR through the logo
theme_note: These codes describe the logo making the subreddit visible, people subscribing and defending after finding it, and moderators or regulars welcoming and orienting the arrivals. What varies is direction: newcomers recount discovery and ask what the room is like, while established participants credit the builders, welcome them, and describe the wider public-radio remit.

second_order: joking that the new subscribers are a pledge drive
theme_note: These passages use familiar NPR fundraising talk—tote bags and pledge drives—to domesticate the r/place influx. The joke varies from asking for a reward to naming the whole recruitment surge as a pre-pledge-drive pledge drive.

second_order: arguing whether playing the canvas game helps NPR
theme_note: This exchange disputes the value of the effort: one participant calls it a silly contest that cannot sustain NPR, while the reply says donating to public radio and playing the game can coexist. The shared practice is explicitly working out what participation is worth, not merely taking opposite positions nearby.

second_order: proposing a script to defend the logo
theme_note: The surviving title alone proposes automating defense with a script. It stays a single-code theme because the record supplies no body explaining the practice and manual defense should not be assumed to be the same thing.
regrouped_from: rallying people to defend the little NPR space — separated because scripted automation is materially different from the manual recruitment and pixel work described elsewhere, and the deleted body gives no basis for merging them
